report.summary: Chunk 2 of 4 of daedalus/structcore/graph.py: defines callees, callers, fenced_fragment, canonical_node, and helpers; includes comments about ordering, safety reachability, and REACH_VISIT_CAP.
risks: callees | medium | Order of hits is sorted by name, which may not reflect actual call order; could affect deterministic output but not correctness. | Check if any consumer relies on call order beyond determinism.
callers | medium | Falls back to name match when resolver lacks import info; may include false positives. | Verify that the fallback is acceptable for all use cases.

fenced_fragment | medium | Uses substring match (f in norm); may produce false positives if fragment is a substring of a longer path. | Consider if false positives are acceptable given the 'err in allowed direction' comment.
canonical_node | low | Uses posixpath.normpath but does not handle all edge cases (e.g., symlinks). | Test with symbolic links or mount points.
REACH_VISIT_CAP | medium | The cap of 5000 is arbitrary; a pathological graph could still exceed it before the cap is hit. | Add a mechanism to detect and report truncation accurately.
todos: Verify that the sorted order in callees does not break any downstream code that relied on the previous hash-dependent order.
Add tests for fenced_fragment with edge cases like empty fragment, overlapping fragments, and case sensitivity.
Consider adding a warning log when REACH_VISIT_CAP is hit.

handoff.purpose: Defines call-edge approximation, safety-class reachability helpers, and path normalization functions.

symbols.name: callees
symbols.note: Returns list of CodeUnit that focus most likely calls; uses resolver for resolution if provided.

symbols.name: callers
symbols.note: Returns list of CodeUnit that likely call focus; uses resolver to filter by import relationship.

symbols.name: REACH_VISIT_CAP
symbols.note: Maximum number of nodes to visit in reachability traversal; set to 5000.

symbols.name: _fence_norm
symbols.note: Normalizes a relative path for fence matching: forward slashes, lowercased, root-anchored with leading '/'.

symbols.name: fenced_fragment
symbols.note: Returns the first fenced fragment matching rel, or None; uses substring match.

symbols.name: canonical_node
symbols.note: Returns the canonical index node for a rel path, or None if not in index; uses posixpath.normpath.

claims.text: Without ``resolver``: pure name match over ``candidates`` (v1 behavior).
claims.why: The code returns [u for u in candidates if u.name in used and u.name != focus.name] when resolver is None.

claims.text: With ``resolver``: each referenced name is resolved local->imported first; only names the resolver can't place fall back to a candidate name match.
claims.why: The code uses resolver.resolve(name, focus.module); if resolved is not None and not focus, adds resolved; else checks by_name.
When resolver is None, referencing is built by name match and returned directly.

claims.text: With ``resolver``: a referencing unit counts only if it is in ``focus``'s file or in a file that IMPORTS ``focus``'s file (dropping false edges to same-named symbols in unrelated modules); if the resolver has no import info for that file, it falls back to the name match so no real caller is lost.
claims.why: The code checks u.module == focus.module or resolver.imports(u.module, focus.module); if u.module not in resolver.imports_by_file, adds u.

claims.text: The leading slash is deliberate and is NOT what ``sensitivity._norm`` does.
claims.why: The function sensitivity._norm is not defined in this chunk; cannot verify the contrast.

claims.text: The generic fence ships fragments like ``/controller`` and ``/safety``, which a repo-relative rel (``controller/hv_interlock.py``) cannot contain -- so anchoring here catches top-level fenced trees that a bare substring test misses.
claims.why: The function adds a leading '/' to norm, ensuring that a fragment like '/controller' will match a normalized path like '/controller/hv_interlock.py' via substring check.

claims.text: It can only ever match MORE than the literal check, which is the direction this whole module is allowed to err in.
claims.why: The function normalizes case and slashes and adds leading slash, which increases matches compared to a literal string comparison.

claims.text: Fragment order comes from the policy tuple (a total order), so the reported reason is stable.
claims.why: The function iterates over fenced_paths; the order of that iterable is not defined in this chunk.

claims.text: Spelling is a BYPASS CLASS, not a cosmetic detail: the fence is keyed on graph membership, so ``Utils/Clamp.py`` (Windows hands back either case), ``./utils/clamp.py`` and ``utils/../utils/clamp.py`` all used to miss the node and read as 'no known dependents' -- i.e. as safe. Resolve the spelling before deciding, never after.
claims.why: The function uses posixpath.normpath and strips leading './' to canonicalize the path before lookups.

claims.text: A leaf that 5000 modules transitively depend on is either a pathological graph or a blast radius so large that escalating is right anyway, so the cap is not a correctness compromise -- but the caller MUST treat ``truncated`` as 'could not prove safe', never as 'safe'.
claims.why: The constant is defined but its usage (truncation handling) is not in this chunk.

observations.what: callees sorts used names to ensure deterministic order, avoiding PYTHONHASHSEED dependence.
callers uses resolver.imports_by_file to check if import info exists; if not, falls back to including the unit.
_fence_norm adds a leading '/' to the normalized path; the docstring explains this differs from sensitivity._norm.
fenced_fragment uses a substring check (f in norm) which may produce false positives if a fragment is a substring of a longer path component.
canonical_node uses posixpath.normpath but does not resolve symlinks or handle case-insensitive filesystems beyond lowercasing in _fence_norm (which is not used here).
REACH_VISIT_CAP is set to 5000; the comment cautions that truncation must be treated as 'could not prove safe'.
